channel.title: One Small Thing on Cullen MacDonald
channel.description: Recent content in One Small Thing on Cullen MacDonald

item.title: take no action
item.description:
One of the biggest-impact things you can do as a leader is make sure your team has a way to reflect on itself. And that they can do it in a (sorry, it’s cliché, but) psychologically safe way is critical to getting anything useful out of it. People need to feel like they can say something isn’t working, even when the thing that isn’t working was your idea.

After enough years, the processes, routines, and decisions about how the team works really pile up. It’s easy to pick apart decisions someone else made, but it can feel pretty bad to hear that something you suggested, maybe something you put a lot of work into, is making someone else’s job harder. If you want people to keep telling you those things, how you respond matters.

item.title: E Pluribus Unum
item.description:
Last week, the thing we changed was what we thought our goal was on a given day. We took the context of Standup, listened to what everyone else needed, and thought about where we could make the biggest impact on the team even if that meant putting down our own work to help someone else finish theirs.

This week, I want you to use that same practice of taking the entire team’s context into account and try to frame a single goal for the team to accomplish by Friday. What’s the one thing you want to be able to say is true at the end of the week? Talk it through together, because the people doing the work will have a lot to say about what’s possible and what they’ll need from each other to get there.

item.title: Ok now I...
item.description:
This week I’m going to ask you to do the hardest possible thing imaginable: changing your mind.

So far, with regards to Standup, we’ve started to notice what our teammates say, encouraged everyone, including ourselves. to pick one thing that matters most and have that be our only goal, and then spent a week making sure to call out what we need from each other to get that one goal done.

item.title: No. Blockers!
item.description:
I tossed and turned about which order to do last week’s and this week’s small things in. Hopefully your team struggled a little with narrowing down to one goal at standup, because there are a few things to coach on there.

One way to get to one goal is to figure out which thing matters most and say that out loud, instead of listing all the things you want to do. Forcing yourself, or asking your team, to rank all the mega-important things on their own scale, so not every item is mega-important, is a useful skill.

item.title: Make a Change
item.description: After two weeks of trying to take a look at how and why your team is working the way it is, I’m gonna throw out the first change I want you to make. I’m guessing that while you were listening and noticing the things your team was saying in standup, you thought, gee-whiz, they sure are listing a lot of things each day. They probably also didn’t give themselves a clear way to notice whether they’d made progress on the most important things.

item.title: Everybody get up
item.description:
Last week, I asked you to think about the origins of a regular meeting you’ve been having. Hopefully you didn’t just think about it, you wrote your thoughts down.

Let’s talk about Standup. The format varies from team to team, but the idea is familiar: get together regularly, share your todos for the day and mention when you need help. Over time, though, a short, frequent meeting can decay in quality much quicker than others, turning into a routine people go through without really listening.

item.title: The First Small Thing
item.description:
Every team has a way of doing things. How meetings run, how decisions get made, what happens when work gets stuck. When you join a team, you learn those things so you can get on with the work. After a while, they can stop feeling like choices anyone made. They’re just how work works.

The trouble is that the way a team works can keep going long after the circumstances that shaped it have changed. People come and go. Customers change. Products and codebases grow. Teams move offices, go remote, and then return again. A process that made sense at a time can stop making sense. If the org doesn’t have the muscle to contend with those pains, then they are addressed long after they start hurting.
